Neonates of the Common mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus) emerge from their gelatinous egg capsules at a relatively advanced stage of development, having undergone a prolonged incubation period. When eggs are maintained at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], a duration that reflects the species' adaptation to cool aquatic environments. At the moment of eclosion, newly hatched larvae measure roughly 2 centimeters [Lb = roughly 2 centimeters] in total length and possess a wet weight of about 0.0871 grams [Wwb = about 0.0871 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores their reliance on yolk reserves during early development. These endotrophic, yolk-sac larvae immediately exhibit the external gills characteristic of the genus and begin a brief non-feeding period while absorbing the remaining yolk mass. The transition to active exogenous feeding typically follows within days, after which the free-swimming tadpoles commence a phase of rapid somatic growth in the shallow, well-oxygenated streams and lakes they inhabit across eastern North America.

Under the cool thermal conditions typical of many mudpuppy habitats, which average around 15 °C [T = 15 °C], growth proceeds at a deliberate pace as the aquatic larvae progress through a series of developmental stages. Field surveys have documented that individuals typically attain the onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, when their total body length reaches approximately 20 centimeters [Lp = approximately 20 centimeters]. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight of a maturing mudpuppy is estimated to be around 100 grams [Wwp = around 100 grams], a value that represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue required to support eventual reproductive effort. The timing of this pubertal transition is notably protracted compared to many other amphibians, with females reaching maturity at an older age than males. Specifically, the time elapsed since birth at the attainment of sexual maturity for females is approximately 2,190 days from birth [tp = approximately 2,190 days from birth], whereas males achieve puberty considerably sooner, at roughly 1,825 days from birth [tp = roughly 1,825 days from birth], with both estimates derived from individuals maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

The maximum recorded longevity of the Common mudpuppy is surprisingly high for a North American urodele, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 12,410 days under conditions that average 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, equivalent to roughly 34 years [am = roughly 34 years], is facilitated by the species' low metabolic rate, neotenic retention of gills, and occupation of relatively stable, predator-dilute aquatic environments at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Throughout this extended adult phase, sexually mature individuals, which have achieved a total body length of at least 20 centimeters [Lp = at least 20 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 100 grams [Wwp = 100 grams], allocate resources toward reproduction. The maximum recorded adult size, or ultimate total length, can reach up to 40 centimeters [Li = up to 40 centimeters] in particularly old or well-nourished specimens, with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 453 grams [Wwi = 453 grams] reported from large, gravid females collected during field studies in the Great Lakes region. This combination of slow growth, delayed maturation, and extended longevity places Necturus maculosus among the most extreme slow-lived amphibians known.

Reproductive output in the Common mudpuppy is constrained by the cool water temperatures that dominate its habitat, and peak breeding activity coincides with early spring when temperatures hover near 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Under these conditions, gravid females typically produce eggs in a single annual nesting event, depositing between 20 and 200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 20 and 200 eggs per clutch]. Because females usually raise only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] in natural settings, the resulting annual reproductive output amounts to 20 to 200 offspring per individual annually, a strategy consistent with the species' slow life-history pace and extended generation times. The eggs, each measuring 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter and coated in a protective jelly, are deposited in a sheltered nest cavity beneath a large rock or submerged log, where the attendant female guards them against predators and maintains water flow through gentle fanning motions throughout the roughly 60-day incubation period at 20 °C (roughly 60 days) [ab = roughly 60 days] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Such prolonged maternal care is relatively uncommon among amphibians and underscores the species' substantial investment in each reproductive event.

Comparative life-history data across the family Proteidae reveal that Necturus maculosus occupies an extreme position along the slow-fast continuum, exhibiting exceptionally delayed reproduction and extended longevity. While the 2 centimeter [Lb = 2 centimeter] total length at birth is typical of neotenic salamanders, the species' ultimate total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] places it among the largest obligate paedomorphs in the world. The gradual approach to the 20 centimeter [Lp = 20 centimeter] puberty threshold is reflected in the wet weight milestones, with the 100 gram [Wwp = 100 gram] mass at puberty representing only about 22 percent of the 453 gram [Wwi = 453 gram] ultimate wet weight attained by the largest adults. This life-history configuration, including a maximum reproductive output of 20 to 200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 20 to 200 eggs per clutch], an estimated lifespan of 34 years [am = 34 years], and a female age at puberty of 6 years from birth [tp = 6 years from birth] versus a male age at puberty of 5 years from birth [tp = 5 years from birth] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], aligns closely with the predictions of demographic theory for organisms inhabiting low-mortality, food-limited environments where iteroparity and delayed maturation are selectively advantageous.
